passage: Lavanya, you heard the shouting from your balcony last night, didn't you? Yeah. That was me, Kiran, at full volume. Papa said I can't apply to the hostel school in Dehradun, and before he'd even finished I was yelling, "You never let me do anything!" He shouted back, and it got so loud Amma shut the windows. I wasn't only angry. I was hurt, because I'd shown him the brochure three times and he'd never read it. Then I did something new. I said, "I need ten minutes," and went up to the terrace. I counted the water tanks on every roof. When I came down, my voice was normal. I said, "I want you to read the brochure before you decide." He read it. He still said no, for now. But this time he actually heard me.

qa.q: Where is the hostel school Kiran wanted to apply to?
qa.a: In Dehradun.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while yelling at Papa?
qa.a: Kiran was angry but mostly hurt, because Papa had never read the brochure despite being shown it three times.

qa.q: What worked better than the shouting?
qa.a: Taking a ten-minute break, then coming back with a normal voice and a clear request: read the brochure before deciding.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Kiran came down speaking normally?
qa.a: Papa probably felt calmer and more able to listen, which is why he read the brochure, even though he still said no for now.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager yelling at a parent out of hurt and a wish to be heard, then taking a break and returning with a lower voice.

subtype: Screams as alarm and help calls [Interpreting]
passage: On a windy evening by the river in Lisbon, Kofi and Ines were walking back from football when a scream came from under the bridge: "Help! Somebody!" Ines rolled her eyes. "It's those Year 10 boys again. They did exactly this last week and laughed at everyone who ran." Kofi hesitated. The voice sounded higher and thinner this time. "If it's a prank, we look silly. If it isn't..." They didn't go under the bridge alone. They waved over a couple walking a dog and went together to the railing, where they could see down. A younger girl was sitting on the wet steps holding her ankle, her scooter on its side. Kofi called the emergency number while Ines stayed with the girl, and the couple fetched her parents from the café. Later Ines said quietly, "Those prank screams nearly made me walk past."

qa.q: Where did the scream come from?
qa.a: From under the bridge.

qa.q: What was Kofi feeling when he hesitated?
qa.a: Kofi felt torn and uneasy: worried about looking silly if it was a prank, but more worried someone was really hurt.

qa.q: How did Kofi and Ines check safely?
qa.a: They didn't go under the bridge alone; they brought the couple with the dog, looked down from the railing, then called for help and fetched the girl's parents.

qa.q: How had the earlier prank affected Ines?
qa.a: The Year 10 boys' fake screams made Ines doubt a real one, and she admitted it nearly made her walk past.

grounding: It shows teenagers taking a scream for help seriously despite past pranks, checking safely and calling for help, and how false alarms erode trust.

subtype: Groaning, moaning and huffing at demands [Expressing]
passage: The power went off at seven, right in the middle of revision, and with it the water pump. Kishore's mother lit a candle and said, "Boys, two buckets each from the ground-floor tap before the tank runs dry." Kishore flopped backwards onto the mat. "Uuuugh. Now? We have a test tomorrow!" His mother didn't lecture. "Very dramatic. Two buckets. Then back to your books." Kishore huffed, and went. His friend Yusuf followed him down the dark stairs. On the third trip, Yusuf's foot slipped on a wet step and he made a different sound, a sharp, low groan, and grabbed his wrist. Kishore dropped his bucket at once. "That's not a homework groan." He shouted for his mother, who came with the torch, looked at the swelling wrist, and phoned Yusuf's father to take him to the clinic.

qa.q: What stopped working when the power went off?
qa.a: The water pump.

qa.q: What did Kishore's "Uuuugh" show he was feeling?
qa.a: Kishore felt annoyed and stressed about the next day's test; it was protest, not real refusal, since he went anyway.

qa.q: Why was Kishore right to react differently to Yusuf's groan?
qa.a: Yusuf's sharp, low groan came with a slip and a grabbed wrist, a sign of real pain, so it needed an adult and a clinic, not a joke.

qa.q: How did Kishore's mother read his groan?
qa.a: She took it as dramatic protest, answered lightly and repeated the clear expectation, without a lecture.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager's groan at a chore as protest met with a light, clear response, and a groan of real pain being taken seriously.

passage: In the small school at Bylakuppe, Aparna stood up to read her Kannada poem. Halfway through, from the back row, came a loud hrrm-hrrm. She stumbled. A moment later: a snort. Aparna's cheeks burned. She finished fast and sat down, glaring back at Tenzin. At break she marched up to him. "You think my Kannada is funny?" Tenzin looked baffled, then sneezed. "What? No! I've had a cold for days. My nose is completely blocked." He pulled out a crumpled handkerchief as proof. "The snort was me trying to breathe. Sorry it came in the middle of your poem." Aparna's shoulders dropped. "I thought you were laughing at me." "Your poem was good. The part about the monsoon." She almost smiled. "Okay. Maybe carry two handkerchiefs."

qa.q: What had Tenzin had for days?
qa.a: A cold, with a completely blocked nose.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when her cheeks burned?
qa.a: Aparna felt embarrassed and angry, thinking Tenzin was mocking her Kannada.

qa.q: What would have been a calmer way to find out what the sounds meant?
qa.a: Asking Tenzin calmly before glaring or accusing; once she asked, it turned out to be a cold, not mockery.

qa.q: How did Tenzin experience Aparna's accusation?
qa.a: Tenzin was baffled and apologetic, since the snort was only him trying to breathe through a cold.

grounding: It shows a classmate's throat-clearing and snort being read as mockery when they came from a cold, and asking avoiding an unfair conclusion.

passage: I'm Sangeeta, and our history project taught me something that wasn't history. On Monday I asked Saurabh, "You'll do the slides by Friday, right?" He was scrolling on his phone and said, "Mm-hmm." I heard a yes. On Friday there were no slides. When I asked, he looked genuinely surprised. "I thought you were just telling me the plan. Mm-hmm meant I'm listening, not I promise." I was furious for about an hour. Then I remembered that last week, when Ma'am asked me a question, I said "Huh?" because I didn't understand, and she thought I was being cheeky. Same problem, other side. Now I ask a follow-up: "So you'll do the slides? By Thursday night?" If I get a proper "Yes, Thursday," I write it down.

qa.q: What was Saurabh doing when he said "Mm-hmm"?
qa.a: Scrolling on his phone.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling on Friday when there were no slides?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt furious and let down, having heard the 'mm-hmm' as a promise.

qa.q: What habit did Sangeeta adopt, and why does it help?
qa.a: Asking a clear follow-up with a deadline and waiting for a proper yes, because a short sound can mean listening, agreement or a brush-off.

qa.q: What did Saurabh think his "Mm-hmm" meant?
qa.a: To Saurabh it meant 'I'm listening', not 'I promise', so he was genuinely surprised.

grounding: It illustrates 'mm-hmm' heard as agreement when it meant listening, and 'huh' heard as a challenge when it meant confusion, with follow-up questions preventing assumptions.

passage:
Dear Vandana Masi,
I'm sorry about Sunday lunch. When you asked how school was and I said "Ugh," I saw your face go stiff, and Mumma told me later you thought I was being rude to you. I wasn't. "Ugh" is kind of my whole vocabulary this term. Sometimes it means I'm tired, sometimes the bus was awful, and sometimes it's a joke, like when my friends and I say it about exams. On Sunday it meant we'd had three tests that week and I hadn't slept properly. None of it was about you. I love it when you ask. I'm practising tacking a few words onto the ugh, like "Ugh, long week, three tests," so people don't have to guess. Can I tell you about the tests properly next Sunday? One of them was actually funny.
Love,
Gurleen

qa.q: How many tests did Gurleen have that week?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling while writing to Masi?
qa.a: Gurleen felt sorry and a little embarrassed that the 'ugh' had hurt Masi, and wanted her to know it wasn't about her.

qa.q: What is Gurleen's plan to avoid confusion?
qa.a: Adding a few words after the 'ugh', like 'long week, three tests', so people don't have to guess.

qa.q: How did Vandana Masi take the "Ugh" at lunch?
qa.a: Masi's face went stiff, and she thought Gurleen was being rude to her.

grounding: It shows a teenager's 'ugh' meaning tiredness or venting being taken as rudeness, and the teen learning to add a few words to make it clear.

subtype: Quiet voice under stress or shyness [Mismatch]
passage: Pradeep, you said this school radio show is about voices we don't hear enough, so, okay: I'm Dhruv, famous for being the one nobody can hear. In Class 8, our English teacher said, "Speak up, Dhruv, or do you just not care?" in front of everyone. I cared a lot. At home, in our family, you don't raise your voice at elders, so a soft voice meant respect. At school it meant I didn't care. And when she told me off for it, my voice went even smaller, because I was scared. This year Mr Iqbal tried something different. He let me read my answer to him first, just the two of us at his desk. Then to a small group. By October I read a poem to the whole class. Still not loud. But everyone heard it.

qa.q: By when did Dhruv read a poem to the whole class?
qa.a: By October.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when the English teacher asked if Dhruv didn't care?
qa.a: Dhruv felt hurt and scared, which made the voice even smaller, though Dhruv cared a lot.

qa.q: What did Mr Iqbal do that worked?
qa.a: He started in a quiet, private setting at his desk, then a small group, building up to the whole class instead of criticising.

qa.q: How did the Class 8 English teacher read Dhruv's soft voice?
qa.a: She read it as not caring, missing both the family habit of speaking softly out of respect and Dhruv's fear.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager's very soft voice being read as not caring when it came from family respect and fear, and a quieter setting helping more than criticism.

passage: I'm Ritu, and last year my voice started doing strange things. In the middle of reading the morning pledge, it jumped up high on "India is my country" and then dropped low on "and all Indians". The front rows giggled. I wanted to hide under the stage. After assembly, Parveen Ma'am, our music teacher, stopped me. She said my voice box was growing, that it was my body changing, not me being nervous or silly, and it would settle with time. She told me her own voice had wobbled for a whole year. The next week it cracked again in class, and my friend Nisha didn't even blink; she just kept listening. That helped more than anything. Now my voice is lower and steady, and sometimes I miss the old squeak.

qa.q: Who is Parveen Ma'am?
qa.a: The music teacher.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when the front rows giggled?
qa.a: Ritu felt embarrassed and wanted to hide under the stage.

qa.q: What did Parveen Ma'am say that helped?
qa.a: That the crack came from a growing voice box, a body change rather than nerves or silliness, and that it would settle with time.

qa.q: What might Nisha's not blinking have meant for Ritu?
qa.a: Nisha treating the crack as nothing made Ritu feel accepted, which helped more than anything.

grounding: It shows a teenager's voice cracking during puberty causing embarrassment, an adult explaining it is physical and will settle, and a kind peer ignoring it.

passage: At the football club's end-of-season meeting, Kishore stood up to thank Coach Keerthana, who was moving to Chennai. He had written three lines on his palm. "Ma'am, you... taught us..." His voice thickened. He cleared his throat twice, loud and sharp, and clipped the rest: "Thanks. For everything. Okay." He sat down fast, staring at the floor. A few boys started chanting, "Speech! Speech!" Coach Keerthana raised a hand and they stopped. "That was plenty," she said, smiling at him. After the meeting she found him by the equipment shed. "Want to say the rest here? No audience." Kishore looked at his palm, then at her, and this time the words came, slowly, with his eyes wet. She just listened.

qa.q: Where was Coach Keerthana moving?
qa.a: To Chennai.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when he cleared his throat twice?
qa.a: A choked voice: he felt sad and emotional about the coach leaving and didn't want to cry in front of the team.

qa.q: Why did the private moment work better than pressing him?
qa.a: Without an audience Kishore could let his voice shake and his eyes water, and say the rest at his own pace.

qa.q: How might Coach Keerthana have read Kishore's short speech?
qa.a: She understood it as feelings too big to say in public, so she stopped the chant and offered him a private moment later.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager clipping words and clearing his throat to hide a choked voice in front of peers, and a trusted adult offering a private moment.

passage:
Dear Gopika Akka,
Remember you told me last summer that my voice would "do the thing"? Well, it did the thing. Today in the science presentation, on the word "evaporation" of all words, my voice went from normal to a squeak like a door hinge. The whole class went quiet for a second, and my first instinct was to stop, sit down and never speak again. Then I remembered what you said: it's just the voice box growing, not a feeling. So I said, "Sorry, my voice evaporated," and everyone laughed, including me. After that I finished the whole thing. Mr Das didn't even mention it. Only one boy tried to copy the squeak at lunch, and nobody laughed at him. Next time I might just keep going without the joke.
Omkar

qa.q: Which word did Omkar's voice crack on?
qa.a: "Evaporation".

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling right after the squeak?
qa.a: Omkar felt embarrassed, with a first instinct to stop, sit down and never speak again.

qa.q: Why did Omkar's joke work better than going silent?
qa.a: Laughing it off showed the crack was just physical, took the sting away and let Omkar finish the presentation 😄

qa.q: How might the class have experienced the moment?
qa.a: The class went quiet for a second, then laughed along with Omkar's joke; later nobody laughed at the boy who copied the squeak.

grounding: It shows a teenager's voice cracking mid-presentation, the crack being physical rather than emotional, and laughing it off instead of going silent.
